legacy_report:
SOURCE: Support-Vector Networks, Corinna Cortes and Vladimir Vapnik, Machine Learning 20, 273-297, 1995.

COVERAGE: 49,510 of 49,510 chars, all 25 PDF pages (journal pp. 273-297). Nothing skipped; references read for origins. The text layer is OCR: prose and tables are good, displayed equations are often garbled. I rendered PDF pp. 9, 14, 15, 16, 17 and 18 and read them to check tables 1-3, eqs. 24-29 and Figs. 5-9. Other equations, including the appendix ones, were read from OCR only. "p." below is the journal page; PDF page = journal page - 272.

CLAIMS
- claim: Ten degree-4 polynomial SVMs combined reach 1.1% test error on the large NIST benchmark.
  number: 1.1%
  setup: 60,000 train, 10,000 test, a 50-50 mix of NIST train and test sets, 28x28 (784-D), no pre-processing, one classifier per digit, prediction by maximum output. Built within a 2-week benchmark. Fig. 9 shows this ties LeNet4 rather than beating it (values under FIGURES).
  quote: "The combined performance of the ten classifiers on the test set is 1.1% error."
  where: p. 289, s6.2.2
- claim: The paper's new contribution is extending support-vector networks to data that cannot be separated without training error.
  number: none
  setup: Theory. Separable case, kernels and the expansion on support vectors are earlier work.
  quote: "In this article we extend the approach of support- vector networks to cover when separation without error on the training vectors is impossible."
  where: p. 276, s1
- claim: Soft margin at sigma = 1 avoids the NP-complete problem of minimising the count of training errors by minimising the sum of deviations instead.
  number: sigma = 1
  setup: Functional (24) with slack variables under constraints (22)-(23), for sufficiently large C.
  quote: "To avoid NP-completeness of our problem we will consider the case of cr = 1 (the smallest value of a for which the optimization problem (15) has a unique solution)."
  where: p. 281, s3 (OCR "cr" and "a" are sigma, confirmed on render)
- claim: C sets the trade-off between decision-rule complexity and training error, including when no zero-error solution exists.
  number: none
  setup: Theory. Framed through the VC bound (38). No C value or C sweep is reported anywhere.
  quote: "one can control the trade-off between complexity of decision rule and frequency of error by changing the parameter C"
  where: p. 286, s5.3
- claim: On USPS, polynomial degrees 2 to 7 all score 4.2-4.7% raw error against 12.0% for degree 1, while feature-space dimension grows from about 33,000 to about 10^16.
  number: degree (error %, mean SVs per classifier): 1 (12.0, 200), 2 (4.7, 127), 3 (4.4, 148), 4 (4.3, 165), 5 (4.3, 175), 6 (4.2, 185), 7 (4.3, 190)
  setup: USPS, 7,300 train, 2,000 test, 16x16 (256-D), centering, de-slanting and Gaussian smoothing (sigma 0.75), K = (u.v+1)^d. Data not linearly separable.
  quote: "1 12.0 200 256 / 2 4.7 127 ~33000 / ... / 6 4.2 185 ~1 x 1014 / 7 4.3 190 ~1 x 1016" (Table 2 rows, elided with slashes; exponents are 10^14 and 10^16 on render)
  where: p. 288, Table 2
- claim: The authors read flat error across rising dimension as no over-fitting.
  number: 30% more SVs from degree 3 to 7; 10^10 times the dimension
  setup: USPS, Table 2.
  quote: "The 7 degree polyno- mial has only 30% more support vectors than the 3rd degree polynomial--and even less than the first degree polynomial." and "Note that performance almost does not change with increasing dimensionality of the space--indicating no over-fitting problems."
  where: p. 288, s6.2.1
- claim: USPS baselines are worse than SVMs of degree 2 or higher, except human performance.
  number: human 2.5, CART 17, C4.5 16, best 2-layer NN 6.6, LeNet1 5.1 (raw error %)
  setup: USPS, collected from publications and own experiments. Pre-processing for the baselines is not stated.
  quote: "Human performance 2.5 / Decision tree, CART 17 / Decision tree, C4.5 16 / Best 2 layer neural network 6.6 / Special architecture 5 layer network 5.1" (slashes mark table rows) and "Polyno- mials with degree 2 or higher outperform LeNetl."
  where: p. 287 Table 1; p. 289
- claim: Expected test error is bounded by expected support vectors over training vectors, with no explicit dependence on dimension.
  number: ratio "as low as 0.03"
  setup: Bound stated for training data separated without error by an optimal hyperplane; expectation values.
  quote: "In Section 5 we will demonstrate that the ratio (5) for a real life problems can be as low as 0.03 and the optimal hyperplane generalizes well in a billion dimensional feature space."
  where: p. 276, s1 (experiments are actually in Section 6)
- claim: Plugging observed SV counts into the bound gives no more than 3% per classifier, against actual per-classifier test error of no more than 1.5%.
  number: 3%, 1.5%
  setup: USPS section. Observed counts stand in for expectations.
  quote: "In all cases the upper bound on the error probability for the single classifier does not exceed 3% (on the test data the actual error does not exceed 1.5% for the single classifier)."
  where: p. 288
- claim: NIST SV counts per classifier range from 989 to 2,765, and degree-4 classifiers still make training errors.
  number: Cl. 0-9 SVs 1379, 989, 1958, 1900, 1224, 2024, 1527, 2064, 2332, 2765; train errors 7, 16, 8, 11, 2, 4, 8, 16, 4, 1; test errors 19, 14, 35, 35, 36, 49, 32, 43, 48, 63
  setup: NIST, 60,000/10,000, each row one binary separator out of the ten.
  quote: "Notice that even polynomials of degree 4 (that have more than 108 free parameters) commit errors on this training set. The average frequency of training errors is 0.02% ~ 12 per class." (10^8 on render)
  where: p. 289, Table 3
- claim: The SVM uses no knowledge of image geometry, so a fixed pixel permutation would not hurt it, unlike the other high performers.
  number: none
  setup: Quotation from Bottou et al. 1994 about NIST, with the 4th-degree polynomial kernel.
  quote: "it does not include knowledge about the geometry of the problem. In fact the classifier would do as weil if the image pixels were encrypted e.g. by a fixed, random permutation."
  where: pp. 289-290
- claim: Moving from degree 1 to degree 2 cuts USPS training errors from an average of 34 per classifier to 4 in total.
  number: 34, 4
  setup: USPS. The degree-1 count of 200 includes non-zero-slack training vectors as well as support vectors.
  quote: "the number ofmis-classifications on the training set averages to 34 per classifier for the linear case. For a 2nd degree classifier the total number of mis-classifications on the training set is down to 4."
  where: p. 288
- claim: The method combines three ideas.
  number: 3
  setup: Conclusion.
  quote: "The support-vector network combines 3 ideas: the solution technique from optimal hy- perplanes (that allows for an expansion of the solution vector on support vectors), the idea of convolufion of the dot-product (that extends the solution surfaces from linear to non-linear), and the notion of soft margins (to allow for errors on the training set)."
  where: p. 290, s7
- claim: Training time depends on the number of support vectors rather than polynomial degree, and is claimed faster than LeNet1 even in the worst case.
  number: none (no timings given)
  setup: USPS, polynomial classifiers.
  quote: "The training time for construction of polynomial classifiers does not depend on the de- gree of the polynomial---only the number of support vectors."
  where: p. 289
- claim: Without kernels, a polynomial of degree 4 or 5 on 200 inputs may need hyperplanes in a billion dimensions, which motivates the kernel route.
  number: 200 dimensions, a billion features
  setup: Illustration, not an experiment.
  quote: "to construct polynomial of degree 4 or 5 in a 200 dimensionai space it may be necessary to construct hyperplanes in a billion dimensional feature space."
  where: p. 275

LIMITS
- Polynomial kernels only in the experiments. RBF machines are described as implementable (s5.2, p. 285), but no RBF result is reported. The note's RBF material does not rest on this paper.
- Training-set values of C are never reported, and there is no C or gamma sweep, cross-validation or model-selection procedure.
- Experiments used a squared penalty, not the linear form behind the box constraint 0 <= A <= C1. Quote: "For the experiments reported in this paper we used k = 2 and solved the quadratic programming problem (51)." (p. 295). The F(u) = u case is derived in the appendix but not the one tested. The word "hinge" does not appear in the paper.
- Support vectors are defined by equality on the margin (p. 279). Margin-violating points are named separately: "the number 200 includes both support vectors and training vectors with a non- zero ~-value" (p. 288). The note's "on or inside the margin" is the broader modern usage.
- Two-group classifier. Multiclass is one separator per class with maximum output; no probabilities or calibration.
- The authors concede only one classifier type was built on NIST because of the 2-week limit. They also expect further gains from problem-specific kernels (p. 290).
- No error bars, significance tests, repeated splits or timings. By my arithmetic, 0.1 point on the USPS 2,000-pattern test set is 2 patterns, so degrees 3-7 (4.2-4.4%) differ by only about 4 patterns.
- Table 2's "Raw error" is not labelled train or test. It is presumably test.
- The NIST comparison set is narrow: linear, 3-NN, LeNet1, LeNet4. No trees or ensembles appear there; trees appear only on USPS in Table 1.
- "no over-fitting" is the authors' reading of one digit dataset, and "as powerful and universal as neural networks" (p. 276) is asserted rather than tested.
- Dated: NIST and USPS are the only real data. No statement on tabular data, scaling or large-n training cost in the sense the note's 100k+ row means.
- Independence: the authors say they "only contributed with results for support-vector networks" in the benchmark, but both are co-authors of the cited Bottou et al. 1994 paper. C4.5 and 2-layer NN baselines were produced "specially for this paper" by Cortes and Schoelkopf.
- Internal inconsistencies, my arithmetic:
  - Table 3 train errors average 7.7 per class (77/10, about 0.013%), not the text's "0.02% ~ 12 per class". The render confirms the table values, so this is in the paper rather than OCR.
  - NIST class 9 has 2765/60000 = 4.6% by the SV ratio, above 3%. The "does not exceed 3%" line therefore holds for USPS only; on NIST the bound still holds against test errors (63/10000 = 0.63%).
  - Bound (5) is stated for separable data but is applied to soft-margin runs with observed counts.
  - The paper says "Section 5" for experiments that sit in Section 6. A.2 says "maximize" for a functional that the main text minimises.

BUILDS ON
- Fisher 1936 (linear discriminant).
- Rosenblatt 1962 (perceptron; fixed features with linear output).
- Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams 1986, 1987; Parker 1985; LeCun 1985 (back-propagation).
- Vapnik 1982 (optimal hyperplane, dated by the authors to 1965; VC capacity; structural risk).
- Boser, Guyon & Vapnik 1992 (interchanging the kernel and transform order, smoothing).
- Aizerman, Braverman & Rozonoer 1964 (potential functions, convolution of the dot-product).
- Courant & Hilbert 1953 and Mercer's theorem (kernel validity).
- Anderson & Bahadur 1966.
- Bottou et al. 1994 (benchmark); LeCun et al. 1990 (LeNet1); Bromley & Sackinger 1991 (human figure).

CODE: none in the paper. Formulas worth keeping (checked on render where noted):
- Polynomial kernel: K(u, v) = (u.v + 1)^d, eq. 39, p. 286 (render).
- Soft-margin objective: (1/2)w^2 + C F(sum xi_i^sigma), eq. 24, p. 281 (render).
- Constraints: y_i(w.x_i + b) >= 1 - xi_i, xi_i >= 0, eqs. 22-23, p. 280 (OCR).
- Dual for F(u) = u: maximise A^T 1 - (1/2)A^T D A, subject to 0 <= A <= C1 and A^T Y = 0, with D_ij = y_i y_j K(x_i, x_j), pp. 284, 295 (OCR, garbled in places, check before use).

FIGURES
- Fig. 9, "Results from the benchmark study.", p. 290 (PDF p. 18). Bar chart of NIST test error: linear 8.4, k=3-NN 2.4, LeNet1 1.7, LeNet4 1.1, SVN 1.1. These values exist only as graphic labels, read from the render, so they are not in CLAIMS and have no text quote. It is the fastest way to show SVM tying a purpose-built network without using image geometry. The captions script missed this caption because it has only a period-style break; the extraction has it as "Figure 9." with labels scattered.
- Fig. 5, double circles are support patterns and crosses are errors, d = 2, p. 286 (PDF p. 14). Shows soft margin and a curved boundary from few support points on non-separable 2-D data. Best teaching figure for the note's support-vector paragraph.
- Fig. 2, separable problem with support vectors defining the margin, p. 275 (PDF p. 3). Standard margin picture. Not rendered, so check quality.
- Figs. 3 and 4, conceptual feature-space network versus kernel comparison in input space, pp. 277-278 (PDF pp. 5-6). The pair shows the interchange of operations at the heart of the kernel trick. Not rendered, so check quality.
- Fig. 8, 14 misclassified test patterns for classifier 1, p. 290. Fig. 7, 4 training errors at degree 2, p. 289. Lower priority: they show label noise and hard cases.
- Figs. 1 and 6 (perceptron, USPS samples) add little.

PROBLEMS
- OCR artefacts are kept verbatim in quotes: "weil" (well), "LeNetl" (LeNet1), "ofmis-classifications", "convolufion", "dimensionai", "108"/"1014"/"1016"/"101°" (superscripts lost), and "~" for xi. Figures were checked on render.
- No embedded instructions found.
- Rendered PNGs are at /tmp/cortes-render/ (p9, p14-p18), a temporary location outside the repo.
